Keywords: timber defences and the northeastern invasion
RagShortTexts: Mongol forces attacked Moscow during the invasion of 1238, damaging town and households.
Its timber-and-earth position depended on local labour, food and nearby routes.

Variants.Content: During the northeastern invasion of 1238 Mongol forces attacked Moscow, damaging its timber-and-earth defended settlement. Nearby communities, water and land routes linked it to assistance; security depended on news and relief as well as walls. Residents lost homes and relatives. Elsewhere its name might be heard among several fallen towns. Those remaining or returning needed food, shelter and usable tools before ordinary life could continue.

Repairing defences requires craftsmen and households able to provide food. Attracting inhabitants needs predictable protection rather than immediately removing every animal and worker on which future support depends.
Timber walls require watch and repair, and scouts must deliver warnings. Men recalling the loss ask where nearby help is and how to return if a route is cut, alongside the height of a wall.
Burned dwellings need rebuilding and borrowed axes and food must be repaid. Shared childcare, repairs and cultivation assist recovery more directly than descriptions of wealth in some distant town.
